checkpoints: Inbound traffic with two NSGs (subnet-NSG + NIC-NSG) is filtered in order — subnet-NSG FIRST, then NIC-NSG SECOND, an AND-gate that must clear BOTH stages to reach the VM — so either NSG denying is enough to block the traffic entirely no matter how permissive the other NSG is.

In this scenario the request PASSES stage 1 (`nsg-subnet` allows HTTPS from the Internet) but is DENIED at stage 2 (`nsg-nic`) because the request's real Internet source IP is not within the internal IP range `nsg-nic` allows.
`nsg-subnet` works exactly as designed; the actual culprit is `nsg-nic` — a rule set up for a different, now-forgotten purpose that unintentionally blocks this traffic flow.
Correct debugging process: don't stop after checking just one NSG — trace BOTH stages independently rather than assuming one NSG's permissive rule settles the matter.

Use `az network nic list-effective-nsg` (shows the NIC's merged effective security rules including the subnet-NSG's influence) or Azure Network Watcher's IP flow verify (directly shows whether traffic from IP X to port Y is allowed and which rule/NSG decides it) to pinpoint which stage is blocking.
If nobody remembers why `nsg-nic` restricts that IP range, the fix is to remove that rule and let `nsg-subnet` be the single control point.
If the internal IP range still serves a legitimate purpose, the fix is instead to edit `nsg-nic` to add an allow-HTTPS-from-Internet rule, rather than deleting the existing restriction.

Problem 1 (cost): Standard Public IPs charge a fixed hourly rate regardless of traffic volume, so 30 Public IPs means 30 accumulating fixed charges every month even with very light outbound traffic — paying for the number of IPs rather than actual usage.

Problem 2 (attack surface): a Public IP attached directly to a VM's NIC still fundamentally retains the ability to receive inbound from the Internet unless the NSG absolutely blocks all inbound, creating unnecessary risk for VMs that only need to call out, and requiring correct NSGs to be maintained across all 30 VMs to ensure no gap slips through.
The redesign: remove all 30 individual Public IPs from each NIC, and replace with exactly ONE NAT Gateway attached to the subnet holding those 30 VMs.

A NAT Gateway is fundamentally egress-only — it never opens an inbound path, entirely eliminating the risk of receiving unsolicited traffic from the Internet at the network layer, independent of whether the NSG happens to be configured correctly.
After the change, all 30 VMs share a single (or a few, depending on config) stable outbound public IP — the NAT Gateway's IP — instead of each VM having its own individual IP.

This shared stable IP brings a second benefit beyond cost: if the third-party API has a source-IP allowlist mechanism, only one NAT Gateway IP needs to be allowlisted instead of managing/updating 30 individual IPs every time a VM is added or removed — much simpler to operate.

Cost comparison: weighing 30 fixed hourly Public IP charges against the cost of 1 NAT Gateway (also hourly, plus a processing fee based on actual outbound GB) — given the very light outbound traffic described, consolidating to one NAT Gateway is almost certainly significantly cheaper without needing further measurement, since the fixed-cost component drops from 30 down to 1.

Verification after the change: from a VM run `curl ifconfig.me` (or equivalent) to confirm outbound still works normally and the externally observed source IP is the NAT Gateway's IP — stable and identical across every VM in the subnet — while also confirming no VM still exposes a Public IP receiving direct inbound.
allow-ssh-from-office must have priority = 100, lower than deny-ssh-all's priority = 200, so the narrow allow rule is evaluated first
Azure evaluates NSG rules in ascending priority order — the rule with the lowest number is evaluated first
Azure stops at the first rule that matches direction + protocol + port + address and does not evaluate any remaining rules (short-circuit / first-match-wins)

allow-ssh-from-office and deny-ssh-all both match the identical Inbound/TCP/port-22 condition, differing only in source_address_prefix (narrow 203.0.113.0/24 vs broad * — and * already covers 203.0.113.0/24), which is exactly why their relative order matters

If the order were reversed (deny-ssh-all at 100, allow-ssh-from-office at 200), an SSH request from the office range would hit deny-ssh-all first and be denied immediately, so allow-ssh-from-office would never get a chance to match even though it looks correct on its own — generalizing to the principle that a narrow allow rule must always sit at a lower priority than a broad deny rule covering the same condition, otherwise the allow rule becomes permanently dead
allow-https-internet (port 443) doesn't overlap the port-22 rules (different port/condition), so its priority value relative to the two SSH rules doesn't affect the final outcome
The only hard requirement on priority values is that each one must be unique across the entire NSG

A Resource Group is not a decorative folder — it is Azure's mandatory lifecycle and scope boundary that every resource (VM, network, disk, etc.) must belong to via `resource_group_name`, pointing at exactly one RG; a resource cannot be created without one.

Deleting the Resource Group deletes every child resource inside it, making cleanup safe with a single `az group delete` instead of manually deleting each resource and risking an orphaned resource that quietly keeps billing.
The Resource Group is where RBAC role assignment, resource locks, and cost views attach, making it the natural isolation unit for one environment (dev/staging/prod) or one workload.

The biggest difference from AWS is that AWS has no mandatory Resource-Group-equivalent layer — resources are grouped only by tags or split across accounts via Organizations, with no hard lifecycle boundary enforced.
GCP's project serves as its isolation boundary, but it sits at a different level in the hierarchy — above Azure's Resource Group.
Azure's full resource hierarchy is Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource.

RBAC role assignments inherit down this hierarchy — a role granted at a higher scope (Management Group or Subscription) automatically applies to the Resource Groups and individual resources beneath it.

Root cause: the azurerm provider requires disable_password_authentication = false whenever admin_password is set on the VM resource; the code sets disable_password_authentication = true while also declaring admin_password, which directly contradicts that requirement.
This is not a Terraform bug — it's a deliberate schema-level constraint of the azurerm provider, so validate rejects the config before Terraform ever calls the Azure API.

Azure's Linux VM admin-auth model only allows exactly ONE method (SSH key OR password), not both at once — the colleague's "key plus password just in case" intent isn't something the platform supports.

Fix option A (recommended): go SSH-key-only — remove admin_password and the fallback_password variable entirely, keep disable_password_authentication = true and the admin_ssh_key block; recommended because it removes the password-based attack surface (brute-force, credential stuffing) on a public-facing machine.

Fix option B: go password-only — remove the admin_ssh_key block, set disable_password_authentication = false, and make admin_password satisfy Azure's complexity policy (12-123 characters, 3 of 4 character groups: lower/upper/digit/special).
For the "what if I lose the key" concern, the correct answer is Managed Identity plus Azure Bastion or just-in-time VM access as a separate emergency-access path — not adding a parallel password.
After applying the chosen fix, re-run terraform validate to confirm the error is resolved before running apply.

Chooses Premium_LRS as the data disk tier, reasoning that a production DB is IO-bound and needs stable IOPS/throughput with low latency that Standard_LRS (HDD) or StandardSSD_LRS cannot reliably deliver.
Notes UltraSSD_LRS is unnecessary unless measurement shows Premium isn't enough, given it is separately provisioned, pricier, and region/series-limited.

Uses azurerm_snapshot with incremental_enabled = true for the backup mechanism, explaining it stores only the delta changed since the previous snapshot — making recurring backups cheaper/faster than repeating a full-disk snapshot.
Notes the incremental snapshot mechanism is native to Azure, requiring no in-VM backup agent.

States the Azure hard constraint that a zonal managed disk must be in the same zone as the VM it's attached to, and that a cross-zone attach is rejected immediately at the API — so an existing disk's zone cannot be 'moved'.

Describes the recovery procedure: take the most recent snapshot, create a new azurerm_managed_disk with create_option = "Copy" and source_resource_id pointing at that snapshot with zone set to the target zone, then attach it to a new VM built in that zone.
Concludes the plan doesn't depend on the original VM surviving — as long as the snapshot exists, recovery can happen into any zone in the region.
Xác định đúng tên hiện tượng: đây là autoscale flapping — fleet dao động scale-out/scale-in liên tục suốt giờ cao điểm.

Giải thích đúng nguyên nhân gốc: buffer giữa ngưỡng scale-out (70%) và scale-in (65%) quá hẹp (chỉ cách nhau 5 điểm phần trăm), khiến dao động CPU tự nhiên quanh vùng 65-70% (bình thường dưới tải thực) đủ để liên tục kích hoạt scale-out rồi ngay lập tức scale-in.

Giải thích vì sao cooldown = 3 phút không giải quyết được vấn đề: cooldown chỉ ngăn hai hành động scale xảy ra quá gần nhau về THỜI GIAN, không sửa việc metric cứ lơ lửng ngay tại ngưỡng; sau 3 phút CPU vẫn có thể đang nằm ngay biên và kích hoạt hành động ngược lại ngay lập tức.

Đề xuất trục sửa thứ nhất: nới rộng buffer thật sự — ví dụ scale-out ở 75-80% và scale-in ở 30-40% — buộc CPU phải thay đổi một lượng lớn mới đổi chiều, để nhiễu ngắn hạn quanh 65-70% không còn đủ lực kích hoạt.
Đề xuất trục sửa thứ hai: tăng cooldown lên mức đủ để hệ thống thực sự ổn định sau một lần scale, thường 5-10 phút tùy tốc độ boot của ứng dụng.
Đề xuất trục sửa thứ ba: kéo dài time_window (cửa sổ tổng hợp Average của CPU) trong metric_trigger để rule nhìn theo xu hướng thay vì phản ứng với một đợt tăng đột biến tức thời vài giây.

Kết luận rằng ba thay đổi trên tấn công flapping từ ba góc độ khác nhau (ngưỡng, thời gian chờ, độ mượt của tín hiệu) nên cần áp dụng cả ba cùng lúc; chỉ chỉnh một tham số riêng lẻ (ví dụ chỉ tăng cooldown) thường không đủ nếu buffer vẫn còn hẹp.

Nhận diện đúng phần review có vẻ ổn: `azurerm_lb`, `azurerm_lb_backend_address_pool`, `azurerm_lb_probe`, `azurerm_lb_rule` đều được khai báo đầy đủ, và `azurerm_lb_rule` tham chiếu đúng `backend_address_pool_ids` và `probe_id`.
Chỉ ra điểm thiếu cốt lõi: không có resource nào gắn NIC của hai VM backend vào `azurerm_lb_backend_address_pool.lab`.

Giải thích cơ chế Azure: backend pool là resource độc lập, việc thêm thành viên vào pool phải qua một resource association riêng (`azurerm_network_interface_backend_address_pool_association`) — không tự động xảy ra chỉ vì NIC ở gần LB hay cùng subnet.
Giải thích chuỗi lỗi dẫn đến 5xx: vì pool rỗng, LB nhận request ở frontend, cố định tuyến theo rule tới `backend_address_pool_ids` nhưng không tìm được target nào để forward.
Giải thích vì sao SSH trực tiếp vẫn hoạt động: SSH đi thẳng tới Public IP/NIC của VM, không đi qua LB.

Đề xuất fix cụ thể: thêm resource `azurerm_network_interface_backend_address_pool_association` cho mỗi NIC (với `network_interface_id`, `ip_configuration_name`, `backend_address_pool_id`), lặp lại cho cả hai VM.
Đề xuất bước verify pool: dùng `az network lb address-pool show` (lb-name + resource-group + pool-name) để xác nhận `backendIPConfigurations` không còn rỗng sau khi apply fix.
Đề xuất bước verify traffic thật: test request qua Public IP của chính LB (không SSH trực tiếp vào VM) để xác nhận traffic đã route đúng qua backend pool.
Path-based routing (/app/* → app-pool, /api/* → api-pool) is Layer 7 behavior since it requires reading the HTTP path, so it must go through a layer that understands HTTP.

azurerm_lb is L4 (5-tuple IP/port/protocol) and cannot read the path, so downgrading to a cheaper load balancer is not a free substitution — it sacrifices the current path-routing capability entirely.
Core framing: 'we need path routing' and 'we're paying for App Gateway 24/7' are two separate problems — evaluate cost and capability independently instead of conflating a cheaper LB with a cost fix.

Direction (a): keep App Gateway but switch from fixed capacity to autoscale_configuration (min_capacity/max_capacity) on the Standard_v2 SKU so capacity units track real load instead of paying for peak 24/7 — url_path_map/request_routing_rule stay unchanged (no architecture change), and at night capacity autoscales down to the minimum; this is the right call when the system still runs on plain VM/VMSS.

Direction (b): if app/api already run, or could run, on a platform with a built-in L7 layer (AKS Ingress Controller, Azure Container Apps ingress), move path routing to that layer and drop App Gateway — considerably cheaper since you no longer pay Azure's separate hourly + capacity-unit fee; this is the right call once the system is moving to or already on AKS/Container Apps.

Trade-off of direction (b): you lose the managed WAF rule set and Azure's other built-in L7 features (session affinity, centrally managed SSL policy), so it only makes sense when the threat model doesn't require WAF at the Azure edge or WAF already exists elsewhere — otherwise, add Front Door/App Gateway back at the edge specifically for global WAF.
Defines azurerm_dns_zone resource "lab" with name = "lab.starci.dev" and resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.lab.name (references the existing RG resource, not a hardcoded string).
azurerm_dns_zone resource has no location attribute — correctly omitted because Azure DNS zones are a global, non-regional service.
Defines azurerm_dns_a_record resource named "www" that references the zone via zone_name = azurerm_dns_zone.lab.name and reuses the same resource_group_name.
azurerm_dns_a_record sets ttl = 300 and records = ["20.10.10.10"].
Adds an output block exposing azurerm_dns_zone.lab.name_servers so the 4 Azure-assigned name servers can be retrieved.

Recommends running terraform fmt -check -diff and terraform validate, and notes both run fully offline with no Azure credentials needed since they only check syntax/formatting and that references resolve.
States that creating the zone does not make the domain resolve publicly on the Internet — the zone is only authoritative inside Azure until delegated.

Identifies the missing step as delegation (setting NS records at the registrar for parent domain starci.dev to point to the 4 Azure name servers) and explains that skipping it means public resolvers keep querying the old DNS provider, so nobody but Azure can resolve www.lab.starci.dev — the classic "zone created but nslookup returns nothing" bug.
